definitions: wetting efficiency = fraction of the external catalyst surface covered by flowing liquid, dimensionless
superficial liquid velocity = volumetric liquid flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, in millimetres per second
superficial gas velocity = volumetric gas flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, in metres per second

prose: The trickle bed contained cylindrical catalyst pellets with a diameter of 3 mm in a column with an internal diameter of 0.15 m and a packed height of 1.0 m. Water at 25 °C flowed downward through the bed, and nitrogen flowed concurrently at a superficial gas velocity of 0.02 m/s. Wetting efficiency, the fraction of the external catalyst surface covered by flowing liquid, was measured by a tracer method at each liquid rate. Superficial liquid velocity, the volumetric liquid flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, set the liquid rate in each run. Wetting efficiency was 0.46 at a superficial liquid velocity of 2 mm/s with a point distributor. A spray distributor raised wetting efficiency at the lowest liquid velocity to 0.58. Wetting efficiency rose to 0.71 at 5 mm/s and to 0.88 at 9 mm/s with the point distributor. Fig. 1 shows wetting efficiency against superficial liquid velocity for the point distributor and the spray distributor, and the gap between the distributors narrows as liquid velocity rises. The narrowing gap marks the declining influence of the distributor as the liquid rate rises, since a continuous liquid film covers the pellet surface more completely at higher rates under either distributor. A published correlation for wetting efficiency in trickle beds gave 0.82 at the highest liquid velocity, and the measured value exceeded the correlation value by 7.3 %. The excess sits at the liquid rate where the tracer response carries the smallest relative error, and the correlation was fitted on beds with larger pellets. Repeat runs numbered 4 at each liquid velocity, and the standard deviation of wetting efficiency at the highest liquid velocity was 0.03. The distributor comparison covers water and nitrogen on a single pellet size, and wetting efficiency for a reacting liquid or a second pellet size was not measured.

prose: The ozonation tests used secondary effluent from a municipal treatment plant with a dissolved organic carbon concentration of 8.4 mg/L. Applied ozone dose, the mass of ozone transferred to the water per litre treated, was 6 mg/L, and contact time in the bubble column was 12 min. Effluent pH was 7.4 and effluent temperature was 18 °C across the campaigns. Removal reached 96 % for carbamazepine, 92 % for diclofenac, 78 % for sulfamethoxazole, and 41 % for benzotriazole at the stated dose and contact time. Fig. 1 shows removal of the four micropollutants at the stated ozone dose and contact time, and the ordering of the four compounds follows ozone reactivity. Carbamazepine and diclofenac carry ozone-reactive bonds and react directly with molecular ozone, and benzotriazole reacts mainly with hydroxyl radicals formed during ozone decay. The radical route depends on the effluent matrix, and the same dose in a matrix with stronger radical scavenging would lower benzotriazole removal before carbamazepine removal moved. Bromate formation in the ozonated effluent was 9 µg/L (10 µg/L drinking-water guideline value), and bromate forms from bromide in the effluent during ozonation. N-nitrosodimethylamine stayed below the detection limit of 8 ng/L in every sample, the detection limit being the lowest concentration the analytical method reports with stated confidence. Sampling campaigns numbered 5, and the standard deviation of carbamazepine removal across campaigns was 2 percentage points. Ozone decay in the effluent sets the exposure available for the radical route, and decay accelerates as temperature rises across the season. Hydroxyl radical exposure was tracked with a probe compound in each campaign, and probe compound decay followed the same ordering as benzotriazole removal. Dose control in the tests held the transferred dose at the stated value, and off-gas ozone was measured at the column outlet in every run. The removal values cover one treatment plant and one summer season, and removal under winter temperatures or in a second effluent matrix was not measured.

prose: The emulsion contained sunflower oil at 10 % by mass in water, with a nonionic emulsifier at 1.5 % by mass. Homogenization pressure, the pressure drop across the homogenizer valve, took the values 50 MPa, 100 MPa, and 150 MPa in the three pressure settings, and each preparation passed through the valve three times. The Sauter mean diameter, the diameter of a sphere with the same volume-to-surface ratio as the droplet population, was 412 nm at the lowest pressure. The Sauter mean diameter fell to 236 nm at the middle pressure and to 178 nm at the highest pressure. The fall from the lowest to the highest pressure was 56.8 % of the starting diameter. Fig. 1 shows the Sauter mean diameter against homogenization pressure, and the curve flattens toward the highest pressure. The flattening marks a regime in which droplet breakup and recoalescence proceed at comparable rates, and additional pressure energy dissipates as heat in the valve. Distribution span, a dimensionless width of the droplet size distribution computed from the upper and lower deciles and the median diameter, was 1.9 at the lowest pressure and 1.2 at the highest pressure. Outlet temperature at the highest pressure was 38 °C. Repeat preparations numbered 3 at each pressure, and the standard deviation of the Sauter mean diameter at the highest pressure was 9 nm. The coarse tail of the distribution carries the recoalescence signal, since merged droplets re-enter the measured population at sizes above the median. prose: Baseline nitrogen oxide concentration in the kiln exhaust was 612 mg per cubic metre, corrected to a reference oxygen content of 10 %. Selective non-catalytic reduction, the injection of a nitrogen reagent into hot exhaust gas to convert nitrogen oxides to nitrogen without a catalyst, used a urea solution injected at a gas temperature of 940 °C. Kiln feed rate averaged 185 tonnes per hour during the trial. Nitrogen oxide concentration fell to 287 mg per cubic metre under reagent injection at the stated feed rate. The fall corresponds to a reduction of 53.1 % against the baseline concentration. Fig. 1 shows daily mean nitrogen oxide concentration across the trial, and the lowest daily means sit in the second week of the trial. Feed interruptions coincide with the weakest daily means, and exhaust temperature at the injection level leaves the effective reaction window during an interruption. Exhaust temperature at the injection level stayed inside the effective window on steady-feed days, and the window narrows as kiln load falls. Daily means weight each hour of operation equally, and hours enter the trial mean only after the injection system reached the stated dose. Dust loading in the exhaust showed no trend across the trial, and the reduction held on days with dust loading at either end of the observed range. points: The vessel holds 2.4 cubic metres of liquid and the feed rate is 0.8 litres per second
Space time, the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate, is 50 min
A pulse of 25 g of sodium chloride enters with the feed at the start of the test

definitions: space time = vessel volume divided by volumetric flow rate, in minutes
mean residence time = concentration-weighted mean of the sampling times in a tracer test, in minutes
tanks-in-series number = squared mean residence time divided by the variance of the tracer curve, dimensionless
variance of the tracer curve = concentration-weighted spread of sampling times about the mean, in square minutes
limits: The method assumes the tracer follows the liquid without adsorption on the vessel walls or reaction in the vessel
figures: Fig. 1: outlet tracer concentration against time, with the peak and the mean residence time marked
prose: This tutorial computes the mean residence time of a stirred vessel from a tracer test and compares the tracer value with the space time from the vessel volume and the flow rate. The worked example ends with a tanks-in-series number for the vessel, and the closing check compares the two mean times. You need the outlet concentration as a function of time and a flow rate measured at the same operating point. The vessel holds 2.4 cubic metres of liquid, and the feed rate is 0.8 litres per second. Space time, the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate, is 50 min. A pulse of 25 g of sodium chloride enters with the feed at the start of the test. Samples leave the outlet line every 2 min over 120 min, and a conductivity meter records the salt concentration in each sample. The conductivity reading needs a baseline taken before the pulse enters, since drift in the baseline moves the computed mean more than any single sample does. Fig. 1 shows the outlet tracer concentration against time, with the peak and the mean residence time marked. The outlet concentration peaks at 38 min and returns near the baseline at the end of sampling. The mean residence time from the tracer curve, the concentration-weighted mean of the sampling times, is 47 min. The tracer mean sits 6 % below the space time, and a gap of this size points to a small stagnant region in the vessel or a calibration offset in the flow meter. The variance of the tracer curve, the concentration-weighted spread of sampling times about the mean, is 310 square minutes, and the tanks-in-series number, the squared mean divided by the variance, is 7.1. A tanks-in-series number of this size describes a vessel with substantial backmixing and a wide spread of residence times around the mean. The area under the concentration curve, multiplied by the flow rate, returns the recovered tracer mass, and a shortfall against the injected mass flags tracer loss to the vessel walls.

points: The vapour is propane at a temperature of 350 K and a pressure of 1.2 MPa

definitions: fugacity = pressure-like quantity that replaces pressure in the equilibrium condition for a real gas, in megapascals
B = second virial coefficient, the first correction to the ideal-gas law for pair interactions between molecules, in cubic centimetres per mole
R = gas constant, in joules per mole per kelvin
Z = compressibility factor, the product of pressure and molar volume divided by the product of the gas constant and the temperature, dimensionless
fugacity coefficient = ratio of fugacity to pressure, dimensionless
MPa = megapascal, a unit of pressure
limits: The truncated virial equation carries one correction term; states near condensation need the higher terms or a cubic equation of state
prose: This tutorial computes the fugacity of a pure vapour from the pressure and a single virial coefficient, and checks the result against the ideal-gas value. The worked example gives a fugacity below the pressure, with the departure set by the sign of the virial coefficient. You supply the temperature, the pressure, and the virial coefficient at that temperature; the virial coefficient comes from a correlation or a databank, never from the ideal-gas law. The vapour is propane at a temperature of 350 K and a pressure of 1.2 MPa, the MPa being the megapascal, a unit of pressure. The second virial coefficient B, the first correction to the ideal-gas law for pair interactions between molecules, is -84 cubic centimetres per mole at this temperature. The gas constant R is 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin. The computation runs in a fixed order: the correction term comes first, the compressibility factor and the fugacity coefficient follow from the correction term, and fugacity closes the calculation. The compressibility factor Z, the product of pressure and molar volume divided by the product of the gas constant and the temperature, is 0.965 under these conditions. The fugacity coefficient, the ratio of fugacity to pressure, is 0.966 under these conditions. Fugacity, the pressure-like quantity that replaces pressure in the equilibrium condition for a real gas, is the product of the fugacity coefficient and the pressure, and the product is 1.16 MPa. The ideal-gas check sets the fugacity equal to the pressure of 1.2 MPa, and the virial result sits 3.3 % below the ideal-gas value. Attractive pair interactions dominate at this temperature, since the virial coefficient is negative, and the fugacity falls below the pressure. A negative correction term lowers the molar volume against the ideal-gas value at the same temperature and pressure, and the fugacity inherits the departure through the coefficient. The truncated virial equation carries one correction term, and states near condensation need the higher terms or a cubic equation of state.

composite curve = combined temperature against enthalpy line for all hot streams or all cold streams in a heat recovery problem

prose: This tutorial builds the hot and cold composite curves for a four-stream heat recovery problem and reads the minimum utility duties from the curves at a stated minimum temperature difference. The worked example ends with a pinch temperature and a pair of minimum utility duties, and the closing check tests the duties against the overall energy balance. The first hot stream cools from 180 °C to 60 °C with a heat capacity flow rate of 25 kW/K, the heat capacity flow rate being the product of mass flow rate and specific heat capacity. The second hot stream cools from 150 °C to 40 °C with a heat capacity flow rate of 30 kW/K. The first cold stream heats from 35 °C to 140 °C with a heat capacity flow rate of 22 kW/K. The second cold stream heats from 50 °C to 120 °C with a heat capacity flow rate of 28 kW/K. The minimum temperature difference, the smallest approach allowed between a hot stream and a cold stream in any exchanger, is 20 °C. Each stream plots as a straight segment on temperature and enthalpy axes, with slope set by the heat capacity flow rate, and the hot segments combine into one hot composite curve. The cold segments combine into a cold composite curve in the same way, and the cold curve shifts along the enthalpy axis until the closest vertical gap between the curves equals the minimum temperature difference. Fig. 1 shows the two composite curves at the stated minimum temperature difference, with the pinch marked at the closest approach. The pinch, the point of closest temperature approach between the curves, sits at 90 °C on the hot composite curve and at 70 °C on the cold composite curve. Minimum hot utility, the external heating supplied to the process, is 2560 kW, and minimum cold utility, the external cooling supplied to the process, is 4590 kW. Heat recovery between the process streams is 1710 kW under the stated duties. The closing check adds the hot utility to the total hot-stream duty and the cold utility to the total cold-stream duty; the two sums match, and a mismatch flags an arithmetic slip in the curve construction. A stream with a phase change breaks the straight-segment construction, since the heat capacity flow rate changes at the phase boundary, and such a stream enters as two segments.

points: Uptake was measured in a fixed bed fed with air at a carbon dioxide concentration of 420 parts per million
Adsorption ran at 25 °C and regeneration ran at 95 °C under a humid purge

definitions: direct air capture = removal of carbon dioxide from ambient air
sorbent = solid material that takes up a gas on its internal surface and releases the gas on regeneration
equilibrium capacity = mass or amount of carbon dioxide held by the sorbent at equilibrium with the feed, per gram of sorbent
uptake half-time = time to reach half of the equilibrium capacity after a step change in the feed, in minutes
capacity retention = capacity after repeated cycles divided by the first-cycle capacity, as a percentage
prose: Direct air capture, the removal of carbon dioxide from ambient air, faces a feed concentration far below the concentration in flue gas from combustion. This study reports a solid sorbent for direct air capture with a moisture-swing regeneration step. The sorbent is an amine-functionalised cellulose fibre, and uptake was measured in a fixed bed fed with air at a carbon dioxide concentration of 420 parts per million. Adsorption ran at 25 °C, and regeneration ran at 95 °C under a humid purge. The sorbent captured carbon dioxide selectively over nitrogen and oxygen, with an equilibrium capacity of 1.8 millimoles per gram of sorbent. The uptake half-time, the time to reach half of the equilibrium capacity after a step change in the feed, was 38 min. Capacity retention after 200 adsorption and regeneration cycles was 94 % of the first-cycle capacity. Regeneration energy was 5.6 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. The retention result links the amine groups to the fibre support, since capacity loss in amine sorbents usually tracks amine loss during regeneration. A sorbent with this retention and this energy demand suits capture units that draw low-grade heat from a host process.

prose: Stationary storage for wind and solar generation needs a battery chemistry that separates energy capacity from power rating. This study reports a viologen anolyte for an aqueous organic redox flow battery, the anolyte being the electrolyte on the negative side of the battery, paired with a ferrocyanide catholyte on the positive side. Energy density of the paired electrolytes, the stored energy per litre of the two electrolytes together, was 24 watt-hours per litre. At a current density of 80 milliamperes per square centimetre, coulombic efficiency, the charge recovered on discharge divided by the charge stored on charge, was 98.6 %, and energy efficiency, the energy recovered on discharge divided by the energy stored on charge, was 82 %. The low fade rate reflects the stability of the viologen radical formed on charge, and crossover through the membrane contributed a smaller share of the fade. An electrolyte with this fade rate and this energy density suits daily cycling duty in a stationary installation.

prose: Plastic waste enters mechanical recycling, landfill, and incineration routes, and the mixed polyolefin fraction from sorting plants fits none of the established routes well. Global plastic waste generation is 390 million tonnes per year, and mechanical recycling handles 9 % of the total. Gasification, the conversion of a carbon-bearing feed to a gas with steam and a restricted supply of air or oxygen at high temperature, converts the mixed fraction to a synthesis gas, a product gas composed mainly of hydrogen and carbon monoxide. Cold gas efficiency, the chemical energy in the product gas divided by the chemical energy in the feed, spans 62 % to 74 % in published fluidised-bed studies. Tar, the condensable organic compounds in the product gas that foul downstream equipment, sets the cleaning duty for any engine or synthesis step downstream of the gasifier. Tar content data for a mixed polyolefin feed at 850 °C rest on single-polymer studies, and no published tar measurement covers a mixed feed with the fines and film fractions present in sorting-plant residue. A single-polymer reference run in the same rig gave a tar content of 8.2 grams per cubic metre of product gas. This study measures tar content and cold gas efficiency for a mixed polyolefin feed in a laboratory fluidised-bed gasifier. The rig runs at a feed rate of 25 kg per hour, with 3 feed blends and an equivalence ratio of 0.28 held across the blends, the equivalence ratio being the actual air-to-fuel ratio divided by the air-to-fuel ratio for complete combustion.

definitions: PFAS = per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, a class of compounds built on carbon-fluorine bonds
supercritical water = water above its critical temperature and pressure, where liquid and gas form a single fluid phase

prose: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a class of compounds built on carbon-fluorine bonds, persist in soil and groundwater near fire-training sites and fluoropolymer plants. Drinking-water guidance in one jurisdiction sets a value of 500 nanograms per litre for the sum of PFAS compounds. Water turns supercritical at 374 °C and 22.1 megapascals, supercritical water being water above its critical temperature and pressure, where liquid and gas form a single fluid phase. Supercritical water oxidises organic compounds in that single phase, and oxidant addition needs no interphase transfer step. Destruction in batch studies reached 99 % for the compounds tested, with fluoride release as the mineralisation check, mineralisation being the conversion of an organic compound to inorganic products. Continuous-flow destruction data for a mixture of PFAS compounds are missing, and defluorination, the release of fluorine from an organic compound as fluoride, has no published value for a continuous reactor. This study measures destruction and defluorination for a defined PFAS mixture in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. The reactor runs at 550 °C and 25 megapascals with a residence time of 45 seconds, the residence time being the mean time a fluid element spends inside the reactor, and the feed carries 6 PFAS compounds. Batch reactors in the cited studies held each charge at temperature for a fixed contact period, and product sampling followed cooling and depressurisation. Fluoride in the effluent, measured by ion chromatography, closes the fluorine balance against the feed.

prose: Droplets formed in a flow-focusing device etched in glass, flow focusing being a droplet formation geometry in which a continuous phase squeezes a dispersed phase through a narrow orifice. The main channel was 100 micrometres wide and 60 micrometres deep, and the orifice at the focusing junction was 50 micrometres wide. Channel dimensions came from a profilometer scan of each etched device before bonding, since etch depth sets the orifice resistance. The continuous phase, the fluid that surrounds and carries the droplets, was a fluorinated oil with a surfactant at 2 % by mass, and the dispersed phase, the fluid that breaks into droplets, was water with a dissolved dye. Syringe pumps delivered the continuous phase at 400 microlitres per hour and the dispersed phase at 40 microlitres per hour. Droplet sizing used a fixed intensity threshold on the recorded images, and the same threshold applied to every condition. The titration cell held 40 mL of a methanol-based solvent
The titrant had a water equivalent of 5.02 mg per millilitre

Samples entered a sealed oven at 160 °C, and dry nitrogen carried the released water into the cell

definitions: Karl Fischer titration = titration in which a reagent reacts with water in the sample, and the reagent consumption gives the water mass
water equivalent = mass of water that reacts with one millilitre of titrant, in milligrams per millilitre
drift = water entering the titration cell from the surroundings per minute, in micrograms per minute
recovery = measured value divided by the certified value, as a percentage
moisture content = mass of water divided by sample mass, as a percentage
mL = millilitre, a unit of volume
limits: Samples with aldehydes or ketones react with the methanol solvent and bias the reading; such samples used a methanol-free reagent
prose: Moisture in the powder samples was measured by volumetric Karl Fischer titration, a titration in which a reagent reacts with water in the sample and the reagent consumption gives the water mass, with an oven transfer step for samples that release water on heating. Each sample portion was 0.5 g, weighed on a balance with a readability of 0.1 mg. The titration cell held 40 mL of a methanol-based solvent, dried before the first determination of each day. The titrant had a water equivalent of 5.02 mg per millilitre, the water equivalent being the mass of water that reacts with one millilitre of titrant, standardised each morning against a water standard. Cell drift, the water entering the cell from the surroundings, was 12 micrograms per minute before sample addition, and each run subtracted the drift over the titration time. Samples entered a sealed oven at 160 °C, and dry nitrogen carried the released water into the cell. Titration ended at a persistent endpoint signal, and the instrument computed moisture content, the mass of water divided by the sample mass, from the titrant volume and the water equivalent. Replicate determinations numbered 6 per sample. A certified reference powder with a moisture content of 3.42 % by mass gave a measured value of 3.38 % by mass, a recovery of 98.8 %, the recovery being the measured value divided by the certified value. The standard deviation across replicates was 0.05 % by mass for the reference powder. Blank determinations ran with each batch of samples, and the blank value entered the drift correction for the day. Samples with aldehydes or ketones react with the methanol solvent and bias the reading, and such samples used a methanol-free reagent.

The pilot vessel held 20 litres, and runs ran at 30 megapascals and 50 °C
The yield gap of 3 percentage points sits inside the run-to-run spread of the campaign
Solvent-to-feed ratio was 28 kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of feed, and energy use was 1.9 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of extract
The campaign covered 12 batches, and each batch ran for 3 hours from pressurisation to depressurisation
definitions: supercritical carbon dioxide = carbon dioxide above its critical temperature and pressure, used as an extraction solvent
yield = mass of extract divided by mass of feed, as a percentage
solvent-to-feed ratio = mass of carbon dioxide passed through the vessel divided by mass of feed, in kilograms per kilogram
limits: The campaign covers a single feedstock; the vessel pressure rating caps the extraction pressure at the stated value; continuous solids feeding was not tested and the claim covers batch operation only
prose: The pilot campaign shows that supercritical carbon dioxide extraction of the oilseed feed holds at pilot scale, with a yield of 31 % of feed mass against a laboratory value of 34 % of feed mass, the yield being the mass of extract divided by the mass of feed. The pilot vessel held 20 litres, and runs ran at 30 megapascals and 50 °C. The yield gap of 3 percentage points sits inside the run-to-run spread of the campaign, and the gap carries no correction for feed moisture differences between the two scales. Solvent-to-feed ratio, the mass of carbon dioxide passed through the vessel divided by the mass of feed, was 28 kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of feed, and energy use was 1.9 kilowatt-hours per kilogram of extract. The campaign covered 12 batches, and each batch ran for 3 hours from pressurisation to depressurisation. Oil recovery at the stated ratio tracks the laboratory extraction curve, and residual oil in the meal sets the economic limit before solvent cost does. Meal residual oil was measured on every batch, and the residual values move with the yield values across the campaign. Extract composition stayed within the laboratory range on the measures taken, and no separate refining step entered the campaign. The campaign covers a single feedstock, and the vessel pressure rating caps the extraction pressure at the stated value. Continuous solids feeding was not tested, and the claim covers batch operation only, for this feedstock at the stated pressure and temperature.

points: For sucrose hydrolysis by invertase, Vmax was 120 micromoles per litre per minute and Km was 0.8 millimoles per litre
A substrate concentration of 0.8 millimoles per litre gives a rate of 60 micromoles per litre per minute
A substrate concentration of 7.2 millimoles per litre gives a rate of 108 micromoles per litre per minute
definitions: v = reaction rate, the rate of product formation per litre of reaction mixture, in micromoles per litre per minute
Vmax = maximum reaction rate at substrate saturation, in micromoles per litre per minute
S = substrate concentration, in millimoles per litre
Km = Michaelis constant, the substrate concentration at half of the maximum rate, in millimoles per litre
steady state = condition in which the concentration of the enzyme-substrate complex stays constant while substrate remains in excess
limits: The equation assumes a single substrate and a steady state for the enzyme-substrate complex; product inhibition and substrate inhibition sit outside the stated form
prose: The rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction under the steady-state assumption for the enzyme-substrate complex follows the Michaelis-Menten equation. The reaction rate v, the rate of product formation per litre of reaction mixture, is the central quantity of the equation. Rates come from the initial slope of product concentration against time, before substrate depletion bends the curve. The equation states that v equals Vmax multiplied by S and divided by the quantity Km plus S. In the equation, Vmax is the maximum rate at substrate saturation, in micromoles per litre per minute; S is the substrate concentration, in millimoles per litre; and Km is the Michaelis constant, the substrate concentration at half of the maximum rate, in millimoles per litre. At substrate concentrations far below Km, the rate is first order in S, and at substrate concentrations far above Km, the rate approaches Vmax and is zero order in S. The equation separates a capacity term, Vmax, from a saturation term set by Km, and a single rate measurement at one substrate concentration fixes neither parameter. For sucrose hydrolysis by invertase with Vmax of 120 micromoles per litre per minute and Km of 0.8 millimoles per litre, a substrate concentration of 0.8 millimoles per litre gives a rate of 60 micromoles per litre per minute, and a substrate concentration of 7.2 millimoles per litre gives a rate of 108 micromoles per litre per minute. Parameter values come from a fit of the equation to rates measured across a substrate range that brackets Km, and a range on one side of Km leaves the two parameters correlated. Product inhibition and substrate inhibition sit outside the stated form of the equation.

points: Membrane: polytetrafluoroethylene, pore size 0.22 micrometres, area 0.014 square metres, direct contact configuration.
Conditions: feed temperature 65 degrees Celsius, permeate temperature 20 degrees Celsius, feed salinity 35 grams per litre, feed flow rate 1.5 litres per minute.
Initial permeate flux 18.4 kilograms per square metre per hour; polypropylene baseline module 15.9 under the same conditions.
Flux at the end of a 12 hour run 13.7 kilograms per square metre per hour, a decline of 25.5 percent from the initial value.
Deionised water rinse restored flux to 17.1 kilograms per square metre per hour.
Salt rejection 99.8 percent across the run, confirmed by ion chromatography.
definitions: membrane distillation = a thermally driven separation in which water vapour crosses a hydrophobic microporous membrane
permeate flux = the mass of permeate crossing unit membrane area per unit time
salt rejection = the share of feed salt that does not appear in the permeate, reported as a percentage
limits: Flux and rejection values hold for feed temperatures at or below 70 degrees Celsius and for a calcium-free feed; calcium sulfate scaling was not tested.
prose: Membrane distillation (a thermally driven separation in which water vapour crosses a hydrophobic microporous membrane) was applied to a saline feed in a direct contact module. The module held a polytetrafluoroethylene membrane with a pore size of 0.22 micrometres and an area of 0.014 square metres. Feed temperature was 65 degrees Celsius, permeate temperature was 20 degrees Celsius, and feed salinity was 35 grams per litre at a feed flow rate of 1.5 litres per minute. The feed circulated from a heated tank through the module and back to the tank, and permeate mass was collected on a balance at timed intervals for the flux calculation. Initial permeate flux (the mass of permeate crossing unit membrane area per unit time) reached 18.4 kilograms per square metre per hour (15.9 kilograms per square metre per hour for the polypropylene baseline module under the same conditions). A vapour pressure difference across the membrane drives the flux, and the difference is set by the two stream temperatures. Flux declined during 12 hours of continuous operation and reached 13.7 kilograms per square metre per hour at the end of the run, a decline of 25.5 percent from the initial value. The decline is consistent with partial wetting of the largest pores and with salt deposition at the membrane surface, and the two mechanisms act on the same timescale as the measured decline. A rinse with deionised water restored flux to 17.1 kilograms per square metre per hour, and the recovery after rinsing assigns most of the decline to deposition rather than to permanent wetting. Salt rejection stayed at 99.8 percent across the run, and ion chromatography of permeate samples confirmed the rejection from an independent route. Three membrane samples from a single production batch carried the full sequence of runs, and sample-to-sample variation in initial flux was small against the decline within a run. The flux and rejection values hold for feed temperatures at or below 70 degrees Celsius and for the calcium-free feed tested; scaling by calcium sulfate was not tested.

points: Biochar produced from wheat straw at a pyrolysis temperature of 550 degrees Celsius, with a carbon content of 68 percent.
Application rate 10 tonnes per hectare, mixed into the upper soil layer of a sandy loam.
Soil organic carbon rose from 1.12 percent to 1.47 percent after application, an increase of 0.35 percentage points and 31 percent relative to the unamended soil.
After an incubation of 180 days at field capacity, 87 percent of the added biochar carbon remained in the soil.

Cumulative carbon dioxide emission over the incubation was 214 milligrams per kilogram of soil for the amended soil against 246 milligrams per kilogram for the unamended soil, a reduction of 13 percent.
Soil pH rose by 0.4 units after application.
definitions: biochar = the carbon-rich solid remaining after pyrolysis of biomass in the absence of oxygen
soil organic carbon = the carbon held in soil organic matter, reported as a percentage of dry soil mass
pyrolysis = thermal decomposition of a material in the absence of oxygen
pH = the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity
limits: Retention and emission values hold for the single sandy loam tested and for incubation conditions; field ageing under rainfall and tillage was not measured.
prose: Biochar (the carbon-rich solid remaining after pyrolysis of biomass in the absence of oxygen) was produced from wheat straw at a pyrolysis temperature of 550 degrees Celsius and carried a carbon content of 68 percent. The biochar was ground, sieved, and mixed into the upper layer of a sandy loam in replicated pots. Application rate was 10 tonnes per hectare. Soil organic carbon (the carbon held in soil organic matter, as a percentage of dry soil mass) rose from 1.12 percent to 1.47 percent after application, an increase of 0.35 percentage points (31 percent relative to the unamended soil). The increase places a large share of the added carbon in the soil pool at the start of the incubation, and the retention measurement tests how much of that carbon remains. After an incubation of 180 days at field capacity, 87 percent of the added biochar carbon remained in the soil. Retention at this level is consistent with a condensed aromatic structure in the biochar, and the structure resists microbial attack over the incubation period. Cumulative carbon dioxide emission over the incubation was 214 milligrams per kilogram of soil for the amended soil (246 milligrams per kilogram for the unamended soil), a reduction of 13 percent. Lower emission from the amended soil held across the full incubation, and the difference grew during the early weeks, when labile carbon from the straw fraction is most available. Soil pH (the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion activity, reported in pH units) rose by 0.4 units after application, and the rise is consistent with the ash content of the straw biochar. Leaching losses from the pots were collected and carried a small share of the added carbon, and the retention figure excludes that share. The retention and emission values hold for the single sandy loam tested under incubation conditions; field ageing under rainfall and tillage was not measured.

points: Goal: obtain the wall shear stress for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe from a momentum balance on a cylindrical shell, with no empirical friction correlation.
Worked example inputs: pipe radius 0.05 metres, pipe length 40 metres, pressure drop 12 kilopascals over the length.
Balance result: wall shear stress is the pipe radius times the pressure drop divided by 2 times the pipe length, and the value is 7.5 pascals.
Check: the shear stress falls to zero at the pipe centreline and rises linearly with radius, and the integrated wall force matches the pressure force on the cross-section.
definitions: shell = a cylindrical layer of fluid at radius r with thickness delta r, concentric with the pipe
r = radial distance from the pipe centreline, in metres
shear stress = the tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals
wall shear stress = the shear stress at the pipe wall
limits: The balance assumes steady, fully developed laminar flow of a constant-density fluid in a straight horizontal pipe.
prose: This tutorial obtains the wall shear stress (the shear stress at the pipe wall) for steady laminar flow in a circular pipe from a momentum balance, with no friction correlation and no chart. The outcome is a single value from three inputs, and the same balance gives the shear stress at any radius as a by-product. A shell is a cylindrical layer of fluid at radius r (radial distance from the pipe centreline, in metres) with thickness delta r, concentric with the pipe. Take a shell of length equal to the pipe length and write the force balance on the shell in the flow direction. Pressure acts on the two annular end faces of the shell, and shear stress (the tangential force per unit area exerted by one fluid layer on the next, in pascals) acts on the inner and outer cylindrical surfaces. The shell moves at constant speed, and the net force on the shell is zero. Set the pressure force on the shell equal to the difference of the shear forces on its two surfaces and divide by the surface area and the shell thickness. The balance gives the shear stress as a quantity that grows linearly with radius, from zero at the centreline to a maximum at the wall. Use the radius in the balance, not the diameter; a diameter in place of the radius doubles the result, and the error passes every unit check. Worked example inputs are a pipe radius of 0.05 metres, a pipe length of 40 metres, and a pressure drop of 12 kilopascals over the length. Wall shear stress is the pipe radius times the pressure drop divided by 2 times the pipe length, and the value is 7.5 pascals. The check is the limiting case: the balance returns zero stress at the centreline and the largest stress at the wall, and a profile with the maximum at the centre would signal a sign error in the pressure term. The result shows that wall shear stress in laminar pipe flow is fixed by the pressure drop and the pipe geometry alone, and the fluid viscosity sets the flow rate that the stress accompanies, not the stress.

points: Ammonia cracking supplies hydrogen at points of use where pipeline delivery is absent; the study tests a ruthenium catalyst on an alumina support for the reaction.
Reactor operated at 450 degrees Celsius and 5 bar, at a space velocity of 6000 per hour.
Ammonia conversion reached 96 percent, with a hydrogen output of 1.9 kilograms per day from the laboratory reactor.
Hydrogen purity after the separation stage was 99.9 percent.
A nickel catalyst reached 71 percent conversion under the same conditions.
Conversion fell by 1.8 percentage points over a run of 200 hours.
definitions: ammonia cracking = the decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen over a catalyst
conversion = the share of ammonia fed that reacts, as a percentage
space velocity = the volumetric feed rate divided by the catalyst bed volume
prose: Hydrogen supply at points of use depends on delivery by road or pipeline, and ammonia cracking (the decomposition of ammonia into nitrogen and hydrogen over a catalyst) offers storage and transport in a liquid carrier. The study tests a ruthenium catalyst on an alumina support for ammonia cracking in a fixed-bed reactor. The reactor operated at 450 degrees Celsius and 5 bar, at a space velocity (the volumetric feed rate divided by the catalyst bed volume) of 6000 per hour. The ruthenium catalyst cracked nearly all of the ammonia fed, and conversion (the share of ammonia fed that reacts) reached 96 percent, with a hydrogen output of 1.9 kilograms per day from the laboratory reactor. A nickel catalyst reached 71 percent conversion under the same conditions. Hydrogen purity after the separation stage was 99.9 percent, and the purity meets the feed specification for the fuel cell used in the test programme. Conversion fell by 1.8 percentage points over a run of 200 hours, and the fall was steady across the run. The conversion margin over the nickel catalyst places the ruthenium catalyst as the candidate for a field unit, and the stability result sets the first design question as catalyst life under start-stop operation.

points: The site stores 48 million tonnes of tailings from six decades of copper milling.
Original processing recovered 62 percent of the copper in the ore, and the unrecovered share reports to the tailings.
Tailings grade is 0.31 percent copper and 0.42 grams of gold per tonne.
The distribution of copper between oxide and sulfide minerals in the stored tailings is not known, and the distribution sets the choice between leaching routes.
The study maps the grade and the mineral distribution across the impoundment from 126 boreholes, and tests leaching on composite samples from each zone.
definitions: tailings = the ground rock residue discharged from a mill after extraction of the target metal
grade = the mass of a metal per unit mass of material, reported as a percentage or as grams per tonne
limits: The study covers one impoundment; the second impoundment at the site is excluded.
prose: The impoundment at the mine stores 48 million tonnes of tailings (the ground rock residue discharged from a mill after extraction of the target metal) from six decades of copper milling. Original processing recovered 62 percent of the copper in the ore, and the unrecovered share reports to the tailings. Tailings grade (the mass of a metal per unit mass of material) is 0.31 percent copper and 0.42 grams of gold per tonne, and grades at that level sit near the cut-off grades of operating mines with richer feed. Reprocessing of stored tailings is established practice at a small number of sites, and the published cases share a common feature: the mineralogy of the stored material was mapped before a route was chosen. The distribution of copper between oxide and sulfide minerals in the stored tailings at this site is not known, and the distribution sets the choice between leaching routes with different reagent demands and different residue behaviour. The study maps grade and mineral distribution across the impoundment and tests leaching response on composite samples from each zone. Sampling covers 126 boreholes on a grid across the impoundment, with assays and mineralogical counts on each core, and leaching tests follow the zones the mapping defines. The study covers one impoundment; the second impoundment at the site is excluded, and the exclusion bounds every grade average the study reports.

points: Silica particles with a nominal diameter of 200 nanometres were dispersed at 0.1 percent by mass in a potassium chloride solution of 10 millimoles per litre.
Dispersion pH was adjusted between 3 and 9 with dilute acid and base, and each dispersion rested for 120 seconds after adjustment before measurement.
Measurements ran at 25 degrees Celsius with an applied voltage of 60 volts across the cell.
A latex standard with a certified zeta potential of -42 millivolts read -41 millivolts at the start of each session.
Where a reading of the standard fell outside a band of 2 millivolts around the certified value, the cell was cleaned and the series repeated.
definitions: zeta potential = the electric potential at the slipping plane of a particle in a liquid, reported in millivolts, taken as a measure of the particle surface charge
electrophoretic light scattering = measurement of particle velocity in an applied electric field from the shift of scattered light
slipping plane = the boundary between the liquid layer that moves with the particle and the liquid that flows past
limits: The procedure covers aqueous dispersions of particles near the nominal diameter; concentrated dispersions and non-aqueous media are outside the procedure.
prose: Zeta potential (the electric potential at the slipping plane of a particle in a liquid, in millivolts) was measured by electrophoretic light scattering (particle velocity in an applied electric field, from the shift of scattered light). Silica particles with a nominal diameter of 200 nanometres were dispersed at 0.1 percent by mass in a potassium chloride solution of 10 millimoles per litre. Each dispersion was sonicated in a bath until no settled layer remained at the cell base, and the dispersion was used within the working day of preparation. Dispersion pH was adjusted between 3 and 9 with dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, and each dispersion rested for 120 seconds after adjustment before measurement. The slipping plane is the boundary between the liquid layer that moves with the particle and the liquid that flows past, and the reported potential is the potential at that plane. Measurements ran at 25 degrees Celsius with an applied voltage of 60 volts across the cell, and five readings were taken on each dispersion and averaged. A latex standard with a certified zeta potential of -42 millivolts read -41 millivolts at the start of each session, and the reading opened the measurement series for that session. Where a reading of the standard fell outside a band of 2 millivolts around the certified value, the cell was cleaned, the standard was remeasured, and the series was repeated from the first dispersion. Bubbles in the cell were cleared by tapping the cell wall before the series started, and a series with a visible bubble in the light path was discarded. Reported values are session means, and the spread of the five readings is reported with each mean. The procedure covers aqueous dispersions of particles near the nominal diameter; concentrated dispersions and non-aqueous media are outside the procedure.

points: The converter delivered a mean power of 38 kilowatts across the winter months of a 16 month trial, against a rated capacity of 200 kilowatts, a capacity factor of 19 percent.
Tank testing had predicted a mean power of 44 kilowatts for the same sea state distribution; the measured mean sits 14 percent below the prediction.
Availability was 91 percent of trial hours, with grid outages excluded from the availability count.
The device rode out a highest significant wave height of 6.8 metres with no structural damage.
definitions: wave energy converter = a device that converts the motion of sea waves into electrical power
capacity factor = the mean power over a period divided by the rated capacity, as a percentage
significant wave height = the mean height of the highest third of waves in a record
limits: The trial covers one sheltered site and one device; performance at exposed sites and array interactions are untested, and biofouling was cleared at each maintenance visit, so long-term fouling effects are outside the trial scope.
prose: The trial establishes the converter (a device that converts the motion of sea waves into electrical power) as a working generator at the tested site, with a mean power of 38 kilowatts across the winter months of a 16 month trial against a rated capacity of 200 kilowatts (a capacity factor, mean power divided by rated capacity, of 19 percent). Tank testing had predicted a mean power of 44 kilowatts for the same sea state distribution, and the measured mean sits 14 percent below the prediction, with the shortfall concentrated in the moderate sea states that dominate the site record. Energy forecasts for the site should carry the measured mean, not the tank prediction, until revised control settings are tested at sea. The shortfall assigns the main loss to the control settings at moderate wave heights, and the settings, not the structure, are the first revision the result supports. Availability was 91 percent of trial hours, with grid outages excluded from the availability count, and four maintenance visits cleared biofouling and replaced one mooring shackle. The device rode out a highest significant wave height (the mean height of the highest third of waves in a record) of 6.8 metres with no structural damage, and the survival case in the design basis is met at the tested site. The trial covers one sheltered site and one device. Performance at exposed sites and interactions in an array are untested. Biofouling was cleared at each maintenance visit, and long-term fouling effects stand outside the trial scope. A second device at an exposed site is the test the claim now requires.

points: Cell: alkaline water electrolysis, potassium hydroxide electrolyte at 30 percent by mass, temperature 60 degrees Celsius, electrode area 25 square centimetres.
Sweep: current density from zero to 800 milliamperes per square centimetre at a scan rate of 5 millivolts per second.
Cell voltage at the highest current density 1.87 volts for the coated anode against 2.14 volts for the uncoated anode.
Ohmic resistance from the high-frequency intercept 0.11 ohm square centimetres.
Curves are means of three cells; error bars are standard deviations, with a standard deviation of 0.03 volts at the highest current density.
definitions: polarization curve = the cell voltage plotted against current density for an electrochemical cell
current density = the current divided by the electrode area
figures: Fig. 1: polarization curve for a water electrolysis cell with a nickel-iron catalyst coating on the anode
prose: Fig. 1 | Polarization curve (cell voltage against current density) for an electrolysis cell with a nickel-iron coated anode, in potassium hydroxide electrolyte at 30 percent by mass and 60 degrees Celsius, with an electrode area of 25 square centimetres. The sweep reached a current density of 800 milliamperes per square centimetre at a scan rate of 5 millivolts per second. Cell voltage at the highest current density was 1.87 volts for the coated anode (2.14 volts for the uncoated anode), and the ohmic resistance from the high-frequency intercept was 0.11 ohm square centimetres.
